# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Background and rationale

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is an established therapy for the primary and secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death [1,2]. For decades, transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) were the standard of care, but their endovascular leads are vulnerable to a range of complications, including infection, pneumothorax, venous thrombosis, and lead fracture or dislodgement [3]. At 10 years post-implant, the risk of lead failure can be as high as 25% in patients with a transvenous ICD. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was conceived to circumvent these problems: it was designed to avoid complications related to the transvenous ICD lead by using an entirely extrathoracic placement.

The feasibility of an entirely extravascular system was first demonstrated in a series of pilot studies, published in 2010, that identified an optimal left-parasternal lead and left-lateral generator configuration and confirmed reliable defibrillation in humans [4]. Because the device has no endovascular or epicardial components, it cannot provide long-term bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP), which constrains candidate selection [5].

## Early clinical evidence

Prospective non-randomized studies established initial safety and efficacy. The most frequent complications of ICDs involve the transvenous leads; the S-ICD was developed as an alternative system, and an early prospective, nonrandomized, multicenter trial evaluated its safety and effectiveness for treating ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation [6]. A pooled analysis of the IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry provided larger-scale confirmation: among 882 patients followed for 651 ± 345 days, spontaneous events were terminated, and complication and inappropriate-shock rates declined with strategic programming and increasing operator experience [7]. Inappropriate shocks, predominantly from cardiac oversensing, were nonetheless a recognized limitation in early cohorts [8].

## Patient selection and screening

A distinctive feature of S-ICD candidacy is the mandatory preimplant electrocardiographic screening to identify patients at risk of T-wave oversensing. An ECG screening test was developed to identify patients at risk for T-wave oversensing, and one study aimed to determine the proportion of potential recipients who fail screening and to identify predictors of failure. Among 100 patients, 8% failed the screening test, and those with T-wave inversions in leads I, II, and aVF were 23 times more likely to fail [9]. Screening failure is more frequent in specific populations such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, particularly during exercise [10].

## Randomized comparisons with the transvenous ICD

The pivotal PRAETORIAN trial provided the first randomized head-to-head comparison. The trial randomized patients with a class I or IIa indication for ICD therapy without the need for pacing to either S-ICD or TV-ICD among 39 centers in the United States and Europe between March 2011 and January 2017 [11]. In this trial, 849 patients were randomized to either S-ICD or TV-ICD therapy and were followed for a median duration of 49.1 months, and the S-ICD proved noninferior to the TV-ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [11]. A prespecified secondary analysis clarified the complication profile: lead-related complications and systemic infections were significantly lower in the S-ICD group, whereas pocket bleedings were more frequent in S-ICD patients [12]. Extended follow-up in the PRAETORIAN-XL trial demonstrated that patients randomized to the S-ICD experienced a 42% lower risk of major complications compared with the TV-ICD arm (HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.36–0.95; P = 0.03) [13].

The ATLAS trial enrolled younger patients and those at higher risk of lead complications. There was a statistically significant reduction in perioperative lead-related complications, which occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) with an S-ICD and in 12 patients (4.8%) with a TV-ICD [14]. The S-ICD reduced perioperative lead-related complications without significantly compromising the effectiveness of ICD shocks, but with more early postoperative pain and a trend for more inappropriate shocks [14].

## Inappropriate shocks and contemporary programming

Concern over inappropriate shocks motivated the single-arm UNTOUCHED trial in a contemporary primary-prevention population. The S-ICD is safe and effective for sudden cardiac death prevention; however, earlier S-ICD cohorts had fewer comorbidities and less left ventricular dysfunction, so UNTOUCHED was designed to evaluate inappropriate-shock rates in a more typical population using standardized programming and enhanced discrimination algorithms [15]. The study demonstrated high efficacy and safety with contemporary devices and programming, with an inappropriate-shock rate of 3.1% at 1 year—the lowest reported for the S-ICD and lower than many transvenous trials [15].

## Defibrillation efficacy testing and the PRAETORIAN score

The need for routine defibrillation testing has been re-examined. The PRAETORIAN score allows identification of patients with high defibrillation thresholds using the routine chest radiograph and provides feedback to implanters on S-ICD positioning, and the PRAETORIAN-DFT trial was designed to prospectively validate it [16]. The PRAETORIAN-DFT trial included 965 patients undergoing de novo S-ICD implantation in 37 centers, randomized 1:1 to defibrillation testing or no testing with calculation of the score [17]. The rate of failed first shocks for spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias was 1.7% in the no-DFT group and 2.3% in the DFT group, meeting noninferiority criteria with a 3% margin [18].

## Limitations and emerging modular technology

The principal limitation of the S-ICD is the inability to deliver ATP. A PRAETORIAN secondary analysis noted that, in contrast to the TV-ICD, the S-ICD cannot provide antitachycardia pacing for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, and this analysis evaluated whether ATP reduces appropriate shocks [19]. The APPRAISE ATP randomized trial further informed the role of ATP in primary-prevention patients [20]. To address this gap, a modular system combining the S-ICD with a wirelessly communicating leadless pacemaker was developed. In the MODULAR ATP trial, the leadless pacemaker in wireless communication with a subcutaneous ICD exceeded performance goals for freedom from major complications, for device-to-device communication, and for pacing threshold at 6 months [21]. This modular pacemaker-defibrillator system consists of an S-ICD wirelessly communicating with a leadless pacemaker to deliver antitachycardia pacing as well as shock therapy [22]. An alternative extravascular approach, with a substernal lead capable of pacing, achieved high defibrillation efficacy at implantation (98.7%), at 6 months, and for discrete spontaneous events [23].

## Current role and guidance

Contemporary guidelines incorporate the S-ICD into ICD decision-making, supported by 2022 ESC guidance on ventricular arrhythmias [24] and the 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS guideline [25]. Meta-analyses pooling randomized and propensity-matched data support fewer lead-related complications with the S-ICD [26], and optimized programming reduces inappropriate therapy across ICD platforms [27]. Real-world experience confirms low systemic infection rates [28], and quality-of-life appears comparable between device types [29]. Overall, the S-ICD has matured into an established alternative to the TV-ICD for patients who do not require pacing, with selection guided by careful screening, anatomy, and individual risk [30].
